talks.summary:
Overview:
Fabian Yamaguchi and Claudiu Ursache introduce ghidra2cpg, an open-source bridge connecting the NSA Ghidra decompiler with the Joern code analysis platform (joern.io) to generate Code Property Graphs (CPGs) directly from binary code. While traditional binary static analysis tools struggle with variable and argument recovery, ghidra2cpg parses Ghidra's decompilation output into an interactive, queryable graph database capable of polynomial-time inter-procedural data-flow analysis. The authors showcase this methodology through physical and firmware-level audits of two 2021 D-Link consumer routers (DIR-X1860 and DIR-842V2), demonstrating the discovery and automated exploitation of memory corruptions, memory disclosure flaws, and authentication bugs.

Key Topics:
- Architecture of Code Property Graphs (CPGs) and binary lifting via Ghidra decompilation (ghidra2cpg)
- Hardware extraction of encrypted router firmware via UART soldering and U-Boot interaction
- Automated attack surface mapping and vulnerability discovery using Scala-based Joern graph queries
- Exploitation of WebSocket stack buffer overflows, uninitialized heap memory leaks (Heartbleed-style), and ROP gadget extraction

Technical Details:
The speakers address the historical challenges of binary auditing where tools like bjorn (based on radare2) failed to reconstruct high-level programming semantics. ghidra2cpg overcomes this by extracting Ghidra's decompilation intermediate representation—which performs intra-procedural argument recovery, variable approximation, and control structure reconstruction—and feeding it into Joern's robust parser. This constructs a CPG supporting full inter-procedural data-flow tracking and graph traversal via Scala or Python scripting. To evaluate the framework on real-world targets, the researchers selected two D-Link routers with encrypted firmware. By attaching a logic analyzer, voltmeter, and USB-to-UART bridge to UART pins soldered onto the circuit boards, they intercepted U-Boot console sessions, bypassed boot restrictions, obtained interactive root shells, and extracted native binaries (nweb and umtfw) from the root file system.

Using the Joern query shell, the authors mapped the HTTP attack surface of nweb by identifying calls to Mongoose HTTP library primitives (mg_get_header, mg_get_cookie) and traversing ten hops outward across the call graph. Next, they formulated a graph query to identify memory copy routines (memcpy, strncpy) writing variable lengths into fixed-size stack buffers within this attack surface. The query instantly identified two critical stack-based buffer overflows in WebSocket handlers handling packets prefixed with init. Because the binary lacked stack canaries and mapped nweb at a static base address without ASLR, exploitation was completely reliable. The researchers automated ROP chain construction directly within Joern by traversing backwards through the control flow graph from ret instructions to harvest gadgets, authoring an exploit in Scala that invoked popen to execute arbitrary root commands (echo owned > /tmp/lul). Further data-flow queries tracking tainted input into fopen and strcat revealed two directory traversal flaws; auditing the error handling of fread revealed an uninitialized heap buffer disclosure bug allowing arbitrary heap memory leakage. Finally, auditing the DIR-X1860's umtfw CGI binary revealed authentication check flaws in 0x88f0 handling HTTP_COOKIE, exposing an authentication bypass in the firmware upload routine (fw_upload).

Key Takeaways:
ghidra2cpg bridges the gap between binary disassembly and source-level static analysis by lifting decompiled code into Code Property Graphs, enabling scalable, query-driven vulnerability discovery across stripped firmware. Combining graph queries with inter-procedural data-flow analysis allows auditors to rapidly uncover both classic memory corruption vulnerabilities and nuanced logic flaws. The research highlights the persistent absence of fundamental exploit mitigations—such as ASLR and stack canaries—in modern consumer embedded devices, allowing memory corruption vulnerabilities to be trivially weaponized into persistent, remote root compromises.
